cards.front: Present Simple vs. Present Continuous
cards.back: Present Simple — routines and facts: I work at a workshop. He fixes engines every day. Present Continuous — happening now or around now: I am working on a truck right now. ⚠️ Don’t forget the -s in he/she/it: he works.

cards.front: How do you make questions in the Present Simple?
cards.back: Use do / does + base verb: Do you work on weekends? Does he speak English? (not does he speaks) Short answers: Yes, I do. / No, he doesn’t.

cards.front: Choose the correct sentence (Present Simple negative).
cards.back: After does/doesn’t, the main verb goes back to its base form: doesn’t work.

cards.front: Past Simple: regular and irregular verbs
cards.back: Regular: add -ed → worked, checked, repaired. Irregular: you must learn them → go/went, buy/bought, take/took, drive/drove, break/broke. Negative and questions use did + base form: I didn’t go. Did you see it?

cards.front: PHRASAL VERBS — daily routine: get up, turn on, turn off, put on, take off
cards.back: get up = leave your bed → I get up at 5 a.m. turn on / turn off = start / stop a machine → Turn off the engine. put on / take off = clothes → Put on your gloves.

cards.front: PHRASAL VERBS — look for, look at, look after
cards.back: look for = search → I’m looking for a 14 mm wrench. look at = direct your eyes → Look at this crack. look after = take care of → He looks after the machines. Same verb, different particle, completely different meaning.

cards.front: “I’m ___ my keys. I can’t find them.”
cards.back: look for = to search for something.

cards.front: VOCABULARY — basic hand tools
cards.back: wrench (US) / spanner (UK) = llave screwdriver = destornillador hammer = martillo pliers = alicates (always plural) socket = dado / copa tape measure = cinta métrica

cards.front: VOCABULARY — parts and fasteners
cards.back: bolt = perno nut = tuerca washer = arandela screw = tornillo bearing = rodamiento gasket = empaque / junta hose = manguera

cards.front: Countable and uncountable: How much vs. How many
cards.back: How many + countable plural → How many bolts do we need? How much + uncountable → How much oil is left? Uncountable words to remember: oil, fuel, water, work, information, advice, money, equipment.

cards.front: There is vs. There are
cards.back: There is + singular/uncountable → There is a leak. There is some oil on the floor. There are + plural → There are two trucks outside. Negative: There isn’t any / There aren’t any.

cards.front: Choose the correct question.
choices: How much fuel do we have?
How many fuel do we have?
How much fuels do we have?
How many fuel does we have?
cards.back: Fuel is uncountable, so it takes how much and no plural -s.

cards.front: Prepositions of time: at, on, in
cards.back: at + clock time → at 7 o’clock, at night on + days and dates → on Monday, on 3rd May in + months, years, long periods → in June, in 2026, in the morning From small to big: at → on → in.

cards.front: Comparatives and superlatives
cards.back: Short adjectives: fast → faster → the fastest Long adjectives: expensive → more expensive → the most expensive Irregular: good/better/best, bad/worse/worst, far/further/furthest This engine is more powerful than that one.

cards.front: Talking about the future: going to vs. will
cards.back: going to = plan or clear evidence: I’m going to change the oil tomorrow. (already decided) Look at that smoke — it’s going to break down. will = decision at the moment of speaking, offers, predictions: I’ll help you with that.

cards.front: Translate: “The machine doesn’t start because the battery is dead.”
cards.back: The machine doesn’t start because the battery is dead. dead battery = batería descargada (not died) flat tyre = llanta desinflada the engine won’t start = no quiere arrancar

cards.front: VOCABULARY — verbs you use every day at work
cards.back: to check = revisar to fix / to repair = arreglar to replace = reemplazar to tighten ≠ to loosen = apretar ≠ aflojar to fill up = llenar to measure = medir to lift = levantar

cards.front: VOCABULARY — numbers, measurements and quantities
cards.back: a quarter = un cuarto · a half = un medio · three quarters = tres cuartos litre / gallon, pound (lb) / kilo, inch = pulgada, gauge = manómetro / calibre How many litres does it take? Tighten it to 90 pounds of torque.

cards.front: Your colleague says: “Can you give me a hand?” What do they want?
cards.back: to give someone a hand = to help. Other everyday idioms: hang on = wait, no worries = it’s fine, let me have a look = déjame ver.

cards.front: How do you say «Tengo 34 años»?
cards.back: English uses to be for age: I am 34. Same with: I am hungry, I am cold, I am right, I am afraid, I am in a hurry. And the question is How old are you?

cards.front: When do you use it and when there as an empty subject?
cards.back: There is / there are = something exists: There is a problem. There are two trucks. It is = describes a situation: It is raining. It is cold. It is seven o'clock. It is important to check. English always needs a subject, even when there is nothing to name.

cards.front: VOCABULARY — describing a problem at work
cards.back: broken = roto · stuck = atascado loose ↔ tight = flojo ↔ apretado worn out = gastado · missing = falta leaking = con fuga · dripping = goteando There is a problem with the pump. It stopped working yesterday.

cards.front: Your colleague asks: «Do you work here?» What is the natural answer?
cards.back: English answers with the same auxiliary as the question: Are you ready? — Yes, I am. Can you fix it? — No, I can't. Did you check it? — Yes, I did. A bare «yes» sounds abrupt.

cards.front: Possessive adjectives: my, your, his, her, its, our, their
cards.back: They match the owner, not the object: Ana and her truck · Luis and his tools Spanish uses «su» for both, so this needs practice. ⚠️ its = possessive (no apostrophe) · it's = it is

cards.front: Which one is correct? (going home)
choices: I go to home after work
I go at home after work
I go in home after work
cards.back: home is the exception: no preposition. go home, come home, get home. Everywhere else you need to: go to the workshop. And arrive takes at or in, never to.

cards.front: in / on / at for place
cards.back: in = inside something → in the truck, in the box, in Managua on = on a surface → on the table, on the wall, on the floor at = at a point or place → at the workshop, at home, at work Vehicles: get on/off a bus or truck, get in/out of a car.

cards.front: How do you ask someone to repeat something, politely?
cards.back: Sorry, I didn't catch that. Could you repeat that, please? Could you speak more slowly, please? «I didn't catch that» sounds more natural than «I don't understand»: it puts the problem on the noise, not on you.

cards.front: Your supplier says «fifty». You ordered 15. What do you do?
cards.back: 13 THIRteen vs 30 THIRty: the stress moves, and that is the only difference. Confusing them is the most expensive beginner mistake at work — native speakers confirm numbers too.

cards.front: Contractions: why I'm and not I am?
cards.back: Native speakers contract almost always in speech: I'm · you're · he's · we'll · I'd · don't · can't · isn't · won't Not contracting doesn't sound formal — it sounds like a textbook. Write them out only in formal letters. ⚠️ Listen for won't (will not) vs want: different words.

cards.front: Verbs followed by -ing: like, love, hate, enjoy, don't mind
cards.back: I like working outdoors. I don't mind working weekends. I hate waiting. But would like takes to: I'd like to learn English. I like coffee = in general. I'd like a coffee = I want one now.

cards.front: On the phone: how do you say who you are?
cards.back: Hello, this is Luis. — never I am Luis. It's a fixed expression. Can I speak to Mr. Ramírez, please? Who's calling? — It's Luis, from the workshop. Hold on a moment. / Can I leave a message?

cards.front: Which sentence is written correctly?
choices: I work on Monday and I start in August
I work on monday and I start in august
I work in Monday and I start on August
I work at Monday and I start at August
cards.back: Two rules at once: on + days, in + months. And days and months are always capitalised in English, unlike Spanish.

cards.front: Spelling: why stopping but hoping?
cards.back: The double consonant keeps the vowel short: hop → hopping (short o) · hope → hoping (long o, drop the -e) stop → stopped · use → used With -y: try → tried (after consonant), play → played (after vowel).

cards.front: Three words that make you sound polite
cards.back: please — with any request sorry — to apologise, or when you didn't hear excuse me — to get attention or to pass by Give me the wrench → Could you pass me the wrench, please? I want a coffee → I'd like a coffee, please.

cards.front: a, an or the?
cards.back: a / an — one of many, mentioned for the first time: I need a wrench. an before a vowel sound, not a vowel letter: an hour, an SUV — but a university, a European part. the — we both know which one: Pass me the wrench. (the one on the table) no article — general, plural or uncountable: Wrenches are useful. Oil is expensive.

cards.front: Choose the correct sentence. (articles)
choices: I need a new battery. The battery is dead.
I need the new battery. A battery is dead.
I need new battery. Battery is dead.
I need a new battery. A battery is dead.
cards.back: First mention → a. Second mention, now we both know which one → the. That pattern (a → the) runs through almost every conversation in English.

cards.front: VOCABULARY — days, dates and telling the time
cards.back: Days: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Dates: written 12 March or March 12, said the twelfth of March. Time: 7:15 = quarter past seven · 7:30 = half past seven · 7:45 = quarter to eight. At work: My shift starts at seven. We finish at half four (British, = 4:30). ⚠️ a.m. = morning, p.m. = afternoon/evening.

cards.front: some and any
cards.back: some — positive sentences: We have some spare filters. any — negatives and questions: We don't have any filters. Do you have any oil? Exception: use some in a question when you offer or request: Would you like some coffee? Can I have some help?

cards.front: VOCABULARY — safety at work
cards.back: PPE (personal protective equipment): helmet / hard hat, gloves, goggles, ear defenders, safety boots, high-vis vest, harness. Signs: Danger · Warning · Caution · No entry · Authorised personnel only · Wet floor. Verbs: to wear PPE, to lock out a machine, to isolate the power, to report an incident. You must wear goggles in this area. Isolate the machine before you start.

cards.front: Your supervisor says: “Make sure the machine is locked out before you start.” What must you do?
choices: Isolate the power so it cannot be switched on
Turn the machine off and leave it
cards.back: Lock out / tag out means isolating the energy source and physically locking it so nobody can switch it on while you work. Turning it off is not the same: someone can still press the button.

cards.front: Word order in a basic English sentence
cards.back: English is strict: Subject → Verb → Object, and adverbs do not go between verb and object. ✅ I check the oil every morning. ❌ I check every morning the oil. Order of extras: manner → place → time. She worked carefully in the workshop yesterday. ⚠️ Unlike Spanish, the subject is never dropped: It is raining, not Is raining.

cards.front: Present Perfect vs. Past Simple — the key rule
cards.back: Past Simple = finished action, definite time: I repaired the pump yesterday. Present Perfect = no definite time, or still relevant now: I have repaired three pumps this week. 🔑 If you say when (yesterday, in 2019, last week), you must use Past Simple.

cards.front: Choose the correct sentence (Present Perfect + time).
choices: I have worked here for ten years
I work here since ten years
I am working here since ten years
I have worked here since ten years
cards.back: for + a period of time (ten years, two hours). since + a starting point (2016, Monday, I was 20).

cards.front: for vs. since vs. ago
cards.back: for + duration → for three hours, for a long time since + starting point → since Monday, since 2020 ago + Past Simple → I bought it two years ago.

cards.front: used to — habits in the past
cards.back: used to + base verb = something true before but not now: I used to drive trucks. ⚠️ In negatives and questions it loses the -d: I didn’t use to like it. Did you use to work at night?

cards.front: First and Second Conditional
cards.back: 1st — real future: If + present, ... will If it rains, we will stop working. 2nd — imaginary present: If + past, ... would If I had more time, I would study every day. ⚠️ Never if I will. The if half never takes will.

cards.front: must vs. have to vs. should
cards.back: must = obligation from the speaker → I must finish this today. have to = obligation from outside (rules) → You have to wear a helmet. should = advice → You should check the oil first. ⚠️ mustn’t = prohibited. don’t have to = not necessary. Very different!

cards.front: “You ___ smoke near the fuel tank.” (it is forbidden)
cards.back: mustn’t = prohibition. Don’t have to would mean it isn’t necessary — a dangerous mistake here.

cards.front: PHRASAL VERBS — problems: break down, run out of, give up
cards.back: break down = stop working → The truck broke down on the road. run out of = have no more left → We ran out of hydraulic oil. give up = stop trying / quit → Don’t give up. He gave up smoking.

cards.front: PHRASAL VERBS — find out, work out, figure out
cards.back: find out = discover information → I found out the pump was faulty. work out = calculate; also exercise → Let’s work out the cost. figure out = understand after thinking → I can’t figure out what’s wrong.

cards.front: PHRASAL VERBS — people: get on with, look after, take after
cards.back: get on with = have a good relationship → I get on well with my boss. look after = take care of → She looks after the paperwork. take after = resemble a relative → He takes after his father.

cards.front: The Passive Voice — present and past simple
cards.back: be + past participle. Use it when who does the action is unknown or unimportant: The engine is repaired every 500 hours. The report was written yesterday. Add the agent with by only if it matters: ...was written by the supervisor.

cards.front: Relative clauses: who, which, that, where
cards.back: who = people → The man who called you is here. which = things → The part which broke is expensive. that = people or things (informal) where = places → The workshop where I work.

cards.front: VOCABULARY — describing a fault
cards.back: a leak = una fuga → There’s an oil leak. to drip = gotear loose ≠ tight = flojo ≠ apretado worn out = gastado faulty = defectuoso to overheat = recalentarse noisy / rattling = ruidoso / traqueteando

cards.front: How do you pronounce the -ed ending?
cards.back: Three sounds, decided by the sound before it: /t/ after voiceless sounds → worked, stopped, checked /d/ after voiced sounds → played, cleaned, repaired /ɪd/ only after t or d → wanted, needed, started

cards.front: CHALLENGE: describe a problem you fixed last week (3 sentences).
cards.back: Model answer: Last week the excavator wouldn’t start. I checked the battery and the fuel filter, and I found out the filter was blocked. After I replaced it, the engine started straight away. Notice: Past Simple throughout, linkers after / and, and the phrasal verb found out.

cards.front: Which sentence is correct?
choices: The parts are delivered yesterday morning
cards.back: Plural subject → were, plus the past participle (delivered). Passive = be + past participle.

cards.front: VOCABULARY — describing people at work
cards.back: reliable = confiable · hard-working = trabajador skilled = capacitado · careless = descuidado willing to learn = dispuesto a aprender in charge of = a cargo de → He is in charge of the workshop.

cards.front: VOCABULARY — materials and conditions
cards.back: steel = acero · rubber = caucho · copper = cobre rust = óxido → rusty = oxidado cracked = agrietado · bent = doblado · dented = abollado brand new = nuevecito ≠ second-hand = de segunda

cards.front: The Present Perfect with just, already and yet
cards.back: just — a moment ago: I've just finished the service. already — sooner than expected: They've already delivered it. yet — in questions and negatives, at the end: Have you called them yet? — No, not yet. still — it continues, and you're surprised: The part still hasn't arrived.

cards.front: VOCABULARY — talking about quantities of work and time
cards.back: It takes about two hours. — duration We're running behind schedule. — late We're ahead of schedule. — early It's due on Friday. — deadline I'm halfway through. — 50 % done It should be ready by Thursday. — by = not later than ⚠️ by Friday = before or on Friday. until Friday = the whole time up to Friday. They are not interchangeable.

cards.front: “The report must be finished ___ Friday.”
cards.back: by = a deadline, not later than that point. until would mean the finishing continues up to Friday, which makes no sense here. Compare: I'll be here until six (the whole time) vs I'll finish by six (a deadline).

cards.front: Question tags — the confirmation ending
cards.back: Positive sentence → negative tag, and vice versa: You've checked the pressure, haven't you? It isn't working, is it? The tag repeats the auxiliary. If there isn't one, use do: You work here, don't you? Two irregulars: I'm right, aren't I? and Let's start, shall we?

cards.front: PHRASAL VERBS — machines: set up, shut down, switch over, turn up/down
cards.back: set up — install and prepare: We set up the new press last week. shut down — stop completely and safely: Shut the line down before cleaning. switch over — change from one to another: We switched over to the backup pump. turn up / down — increase or reduce: Turn the pressure down a bit. back up — support, or make a copy: Back up the settings first.

cards.front: How do you make a polite request in English?
cards.back: From direct to very polite: Send me the invoice. — an order, sounds rude to a colleague Can you send me the invoice? — normal, informal Could you send me the invoice, please? — polite, safe everywhere Would you mind sending me the invoice? — very polite ⚠️ After Would you mind comes -ing, and «yes» means no, I won't — answer Not at all.

cards.front: “We had to ___ the meeting because the client couldn't come.”
cards.back: put off = postpone. The meeting has been put off until Monday. put on = wear · put up = build or accommodate · put down = place on a surface, or write down.

cards.front: Sounds that Spanish speakers need to separate
cards.back: ship / sheep — short ɪ vs long iː. It's a big sheet vs a big shit: worth getting right. s- at the start — English has no e before it: Spain, not Espain. Practise: school, street, stop, Spanish. b / v — the v touches the top teeth to the lower lip: very, not bery. -ed endings add a syllable only after t or d: wanted (2 syll.) but worked (1 syll.).

cards.front: Present Perfect Simple vs. Continuous
cards.back: Simple — focus on the result, how many: I’ve repaired three engines today. Continuous — focus on the activity and its duration: I’ve been repairing engines all morning. (that’s why I’m dirty) State verbs (know, be, have, believe) don’t take the continuous: I’ve been knowing ❌

cards.front: Third Conditional — regret about the past
cards.back: If + had + past participle, ... would have + past participle If I had checked the oil, the engine wouldn’t have seized. Spoken form: If I’d checked… I wouldn’t’ve… It describes something that did not happen.

cards.front: Reported Speech — what changes?
cards.back: Tenses shift one step back: present → past · past → past perfect · will → would · can → could “I am busy.” → He said he was busy. “I saw it.” → He said he had seen it. Also change: tomorrow → the next day, here → there, this → that.

cards.front: Report this: “I will call you tomorrow.”
choices: He said he would call me the next day
He said he will call me tomorrow
He said he would call me tomorrow
He says he would call me the next day
cards.back: will → would and tomorrow → the next day, because you are reporting later, from a different moment.

cards.front: Modals of deduction: must / might / can’t have
cards.back: must be = I’m almost sure it’s true → It must be the alternator. might / could be = it’s possible → It might be a vacuum leak. can’t be = I’m sure it isn’t → It can’t be the battery; it’s new. About the past, add have: The seal must have failed under pressure.

cards.front: Gerund or infinitive after a verb?
cards.back: + -ing: enjoy, avoid, finish, keep, suggest, mind, practise I avoid working in the rain. + to: decide, hope, need, want, manage, offer, refuse I managed to fix it. Both, different meaning: I stopped smoking (quit) vs. I stopped to smoke (paused in order to).

cards.front: wish and if only
cards.back: Present regret: wish + past → I wish I had more time. Past regret: wish + past perfect → I wish I had studied English earlier. Annoyance with others: wish + would → I wish they would stop making that noise.

cards.front: PHRASAL VERBS — work: carry out, take on, set up, put off
cards.back: carry out = perform (a task, an inspection) → We carried out a full inspection. take on = accept work / hire → They took on two new mechanics. set up = establish, prepare → Set up the equipment before starting. put off = postpone → Don’t put off the service.

cards.front: PHRASAL VERBS — put up with, get away with, come up with
cards.back: put up with = tolerate → I can’t put up with that noise. get away with = escape punishment → He got away with a warning. come up with = invent, produce an idea → She came up with a solution. These are three-word phrasal verbs: never separate them.

cards.front: Are phrasal verbs separable? The pronoun rule
cards.back: Separable: Turn off the engine = Turn the engine off. 🔑 With a pronoun you MUST separate: Turn it off ✅ / Turn off it ❌ Inseparable (usually with a preposition): look after the machine → look after it, never look it after.

cards.front: Which one is correct?
choices: I’ll pick up it up tomorrow
cards.back: With a pronoun the phrasal verb must be split: pick it up.

cards.front: look forward to — the classic trap
cards.back: After to here you need a noun or -ing, because this to is a preposition, not an infinitive: I look forward to hearing from you. ✅ I look forward to hear from you. ❌ Same pattern: be used to, get used to → I’m used to working long hours.

cards.front: VOCABULARY — common collocations at work
cards.back: make a decision, a mistake, progress, an effort do the work, a job, research, damage take responsibility, a break, a risk, measurements meet a deadline, a requirement run a test, a business, a machine

cards.front: VOCABULARY — false friends that catch Spanish speakers
cards.back: actually = in fact (≠ actualmente = currently) eventually = finally, in the end (≠ eventualmente = occasionally) sensible = with good judgement (≠ sensible = sensitive) assist = help (≠ asistir a = attend) realize = notice (≠ realizar = carry out)

cards.front: CHALLENGE: write a short work email asking for a spare part.
cards.back: Model: Dear Mr. Ramírez, I am writing to request a quotation for a hydraulic pump seal kit for a CAT 320D. Could you please confirm availability and delivery time? I look forward to hearing from you. Kind regards, Luis Formal markers: I am writing to…, Could you please…, Kind regards.

cards.front: WORD FORMATION — build the family, not just the word
cards.back: From one root you get four words: maintain (v) → maintenance (n) → maintainable (adj) reliable (adj) → reliability (n) → unreliable (opposite) safe → safety → unsafe → safely Common suffixes: -tion, -ment, -ity, -ness (nouns) · -able, -ive, -ous (adjectives)

cards.front: Complete: “The pump is highly ___ if you service it properly.”
cards.back: After is highly you need an adjective: reliable. Reliability is the noun, reliably the adverb.

cards.front: VOCABULARY — precise verbs instead of vague ones
cards.back: Replace weak verbs to sound competent: get better → improve go up / go down → increase / decrease find → identify / detect check → inspect / verify make sure → ensure tell → report / inform

cards.front: The passive with get, and when to choose the passive at all
cards.back: get + participle is the spoken, informal passive, usually for something unplanned: The pump got damaged during transport. Use the passive when: • The agent is unknown or irrelevant: The valve was replaced in 2022. • You want to avoid blaming: A mistake was made instead of You made a mistake. • The object is the topic: The engine was inspected, cleaned and reassembled. ⚠️ Overusing it makes writing vague. In a report, name the agent when you know it.

cards.front: VOCABULARY — talking about cause without repeating because
cards.back: The failure was caused by contaminated fuel. Contaminated fuel led to the failure. The failure was due to / owing to contamination. As a result of the contamination, the injectors clogged. The injectors clogged; consequently, the engine lost power. The leak gave rise to a pressure drop. ⚠️ due to + noun, because + a full clause: due to the delay vs because it was delayed.

cards.front: Choose the correct sentence. (would rather)
choices: I'd rather you didn't touch that setting
I'd rather you don't touch that setting
I'd rather you not touching that setting
I'd rather that you won't touch that setting
cards.back: would rather + subject + past tense expresses a present preference about someone else's behaviour: I'd rather you came tomorrow. With no change of subject it takes the bare infinitive: I'd rather go tomorrow.

cards.front: make, let, have and get someone do something
cards.back: make + bare infinitive — force: They made me sign the form. let + bare infinitive — permit: They let me leave early. have + bare infinitive — arrange, as a boss: I'll have someone check it. get + to-infinitive — persuade: I got him to check it. And the very common have something done (a service you pay for): I had the brakes replaced yesterday. — not by you

cards.front: CHALLENGE: report a delay to a client in three sentences
cards.back: A structure that always works: fact → cause → solution with a date. I'm writing to let you know that the delivery scheduled for 14 May will be delayed. This is due to a shortage of hydraulic seals from our supplier, which affected the whole batch. We now expect to ship by 21 May, and I'll confirm the tracking number as soon as it's dispatched. Why it works: the bad news comes first (nobody has to hunt for it), the cause is factual rather than defensive, and it ends with a commitment the reader can act on.

cards.front: Inversion for emphasis
cards.back: When a negative or limiting adverbial starts the sentence, the subject and auxiliary swap — like a question: Never have I seen such a badly maintained machine. Not only did they ignore the alarm, but they also kept working. Rarely does a failure happen without warning. Use it sparingly: it is formal and dramatic.

cards.front: Mixed conditionals
cards.back: Mixing time frames: Past condition → present result: If I had studied English at school, I would be working abroad now. Present condition → past result: If I were more careful, I wouldn’t have made that mistake.

cards.front: Cleft sentences — putting the spotlight on one part
cards.back: It-cleft: It was the seal that failed, not the pump. What-cleft: What caused the failure was contaminated oil. All-cleft: All I need is a torque wrench. They let you correct, contrast or emphasise without raising your voice.

cards.front: Choose the correctly inverted sentence.
choices: Not until the engine cooled down did we open the radiator
Not until the engine cooled down we opened the radiator
Not until the engine cooled down we did open the radiator
Not until did the engine cool down we opened the radiator
cards.back: The inversion happens in the main clause (did we open), never inside the not until clause itself.

cards.front: The mandative subjunctive
cards.back: After verbs and adjectives of demand or recommendation, use the bare infinitive — no -s, no tense: The manual recommends that the filter be replaced every 500 hours. They insisted that he attend the safety briefing. It is essential that everyone wear a helmet.

cards.front: Hedging — how professionals sound careful
cards.back: Instead of a bare claim, soften it: The failure appears to have been caused by contamination. This would suggest a problem with the relief valve. There is a strong likelihood that… The evidence points to a seal failure. Hedging shows judgement, not weakness — essential in reports.

cards.front: PHRASAL VERBS (C1) — boil down to, iron out, hammer out
cards.back: boil down to = to reduce to the essential point → It all boils down to poor maintenance. iron out = to resolve small problems → We ironed out the last issues. hammer out = to reach an agreement after hard discussion → They hammered out a new contract.

cards.front: PHRASAL VERBS (C1) — gloss over, weigh up, wind up, tide over
cards.back: gloss over = to avoid dealing with something properly → The report glossed over the safety failures. weigh up = to consider carefully → We weighed up the options. wind up = to end up (in a situation); to close a business → We wound up working all night. tide (someone) over = to help until things improve → This will tide us over until payday.

cards.front: PHRASAL VERBS (C1) — technical reports: account for, rule out, follow up, phase out
cards.back: account for = to explain or represent a proportion → Wear accounts for 60% of failures. rule out = to eliminate a possibility → We ruled out an electrical fault. follow up = to take further action → I’ll follow up with the supplier. phase out = to withdraw gradually → They are phasing out that model.

cards.front: “The investigation ___ mechanical failure as the cause.”
cards.back: rule out = to eliminate something as a possibility. The opposite idea is to point to or to attribute the failure to.

cards.front: Nominalisation — the mark of formal written English
cards.back: Turn verbs into nouns to sound objective and compact: They inspected the machine and it failed. → The inspection revealed a failure. We decided to replace it because it was worn. → The decision to replace it was based on wear. Useful in reports; overused, it becomes unreadable bureaucratic prose.

cards.front: Discourse markers that organise an argument
cards.back: Adding: moreover, furthermore, what is more Contrasting: however, nevertheless, that said, whereas Consequence: consequently, hence, as a result Conceding: admittedly, granted, even so Concluding: overall, on balance, all things considered

cards.front: Idiomatic vocabulary for problems at work
cards.back: a bottleneck = the point that slows everything down a workaround = a temporary solution a stopgap = a short-term fix root cause = the underlying cause downtime = time a machine is out of service backlog = accumulated pending work to cut corners = to do things badly to save time or money

cards.front: CHALLENGE: explain a root cause in formal English (3–4 sentences).
cards.back: Model: The failure appears to have originated in the hydraulic circuit rather than the pump itself. Analysis of the oil sample revealed a high silicon content, which points to contamination through a damaged air filter. Had the filter been replaced at the scheduled interval, the damage would most likely have been avoided. We therefore recommend that the servicing schedule be reviewed. Spot: hedging, a cleft-like contrast, inverted third conditional (Had the filter been…) and the subjunctive (be reviewed).

cards.front: REGISTER — the same idea, three levels of formality
cards.back: Informal: The engine packed up. Neutral: The engine broke down. Formal: The engine suffered a catastrophic failure. More pairs: ask for → request · put off → postpone · find out → ascertain · get rid of → eliminate. Phrasal verbs are usually the informal half of the pair.

cards.front: VOCABULARY — shades of meaning in “broken”
cards.back: faulty = works badly, has a defect defective = faulty from manufacture worn = degraded by normal use damaged = harmed by an external event seized = locked solid, won’t move obsolete = still works, but no longer supported Choosing the right one tells the whole story of a failure in a single word.

cards.front: Participle clauses — writing two ideas in one line
cards.back: Having checked the pressure, we replaced the valve. (after doing it) Working under load, the pump overheats. (while doing it) Damaged by vibration, the bracket failed. (passive) The hidden subject must be the same as the main clause. Otherwise you get a dangling participle: ❌ Having replaced the seal, the machine worked. (the machine didn't replace it) ✅ Having replaced the seal, we saw the machine work.

cards.front: The passive with reporting verbs — the impersonal report
cards.back: It is believed that the seal failed. The seal is believed to have failed. Both avoid naming who believes it: standard in reports and investigations, where blame is not the point. Others: is said to · is thought to · is expected to · is reported to. Past reference takes the perfect infinitive: is believed to have failed.

cards.front: VOCABULARY — the language of cause and consequence
cards.back: Cause → effect: led to · resulted in · brought about · gave rise to · triggered Effect → cause: resulted from · stemmed from · was attributable to · arose from Contribution, not the whole cause: contributed to · was a factor in · compounded The overload gave rise to excessive heat, which in turn brought about premature wear. Note: result in = cause; result from = be caused by. Mixing them reverses your sentence.

cards.front: Choose the sentence a professional report would use.
choices: Had the filter been replaced on time, the failure would not have occurred.
If the filter was replaced on time, the failure would not happen.
If the filter would have been replaced, the failure not occurred.
When the filter is replaced on time, the failure would not have occurred.
cards.back: Had + past participle is the inverted third conditional: formal, and very common in written reports. Two rules it respects: if never takes would, and a past unreal result needs would have + participle.

cards.front: PHRASAL VERBS (C1) — meetings and decisions: talk through, push back, sign off on, walk back
cards.back: talk through = discuss in detail → Let's talk the plan through before Friday. push back (on) = disagree, resist → The team pushed back on the deadline. sign off on = approve formally → Who signs off on the budget? walk back = withdraw something you said → He walked back his estimate after seeing the data. Also: circle back (return to a topic), flag up (raise an issue early).

cards.front: Which vs that, and the comma that changes the meaning
cards.back: Defining (no comma, that or which): The pumps that failed were replaced. — only those ones. Non-defining (commas, only which): The pumps, which failed, were replaced. — all of them failed. The comma is not decoration: it decides whether you replaced two pumps or the whole fleet. For people: who; never that after a comma.

cards.front: Softening bad news in writing
cards.back: Direct: We can't deliver on Friday. Professional: Unfortunately, we won't be able to deliver on Friday. Most diplomatic: I'm afraid Friday is looking unlikely — would Monday work for you? Three moves: an apologetic opener (I'm afraid · Unfortunately · Regrettably), a distancing verb (looks like · seems · appears) and, always, an alternative. Bad news without an option reads as a wall.

cards.front: VOCABULARY — precision about quantity and change
cards.back: Small change: a slight/marginal increase · edged up · tailed off Big change: a sharp/steep rise · soared · plummeted Steady: a steady/gradual decline · levelled off · plateaued Approximation: roughly · in the region of · just under · upwards of Downtime edged up in March, then plateaued at just under 40 hours. Adverb before adjective: a sharply higher figure, not a sharp higher figure.

cards.front: Complete: “The delay was largely ___ a shortage of spare parts.”
cards.back: attributable to = that can be explained by. The delay was attributable to a shortage. attributed by would need a person doing the attributing. resulted in points the other way (cause → effect), and due of doesn't exist: it's due to.

cards.front: Emphasis without shouting: what-clauses and do
cards.back: What surprised us was the cost, not the delay. What we need is a second pump. The vibration did stop after the alignment. (auxiliary do for emphasis) It was only after the third test that the fault appeared. In writing you have no tone of voice; these structures are how English puts stress on the page. Use one per paragraph — more than that and the emphasis stops working.

cards.front: The four-line structure of a professional email
cards.back: 1. Purpose — I'm writing to confirm the delivery date for the hydraulic kit. 2. Context — As discussed on Tuesday, the original date was 12 March. 3. Request or action — Could you confirm whether the revised date works on your side? 4. Close — Happy to call if that's easier. Best regards, … One idea per paragraph, the request in its own line, and never bury the ask at the bottom: most people read the first two lines and the last one.

cards.front: VOCABULARY — verbs that make a report sound expert
cards.back: establish (find out for certain) · ascertain (formal version) · corroborate (confirm with other evidence) · preclude (make impossible) · mitigate (reduce the harm) · warrant (justify) · defer (postpone deliberately) · escalate (pass to a higher level) The evidence did not corroborate the operator's account, but the wear pattern warrants a full inspection. Careful: mitigate ≠ militate, and it's mitigate against only in the second one.

cards.front: Fronting and end-weight — controlling what the reader notices
cards.back: English puts known information first and the new, heavy information last. Attached is the full inspection report. — the report is the news Of particular concern is the state of the bearings. End-weight: move long phrases to the end. ❌ That the seals had never been replaced became clear. ✅ It became clear that the seals had never been replaced. This single habit is most of what separates fluent written English from grammatically correct but awkward English.

cards.front: VOCABULARY — expressing degrees of certainty in writing
cards.back: From strongest to weakest: The evidence demonstrates that… — proven The data strongly suggests… — confident This is likely to have been caused by… — probable It appears that… / This would suggest… — cautious It is conceivable that… — possible but unsupported We cannot rule out the possibility that… — no evidence either way ⚠️ In a technical report, overstating certainty is the fastest way to lose credibility.

cards.front: Which sentence is correct? (No sooner…)
choices: No sooner had we restarted the line than the alarm went off
No sooner we restarted the line than the alarm went off
No sooner had we restarted the line when the alarm went off
No sooner did we restart the line that the alarm went off
cards.back: No sooner triggers inversion (had we) and pairs with than, never when or that. Its cousin: Hardly had we restarted the line when the alarm went off — hardly/scarcely take when.

cards.front: PHRASAL VERBS (C1) — projects: scale back, roll out, factor in, bring forward
cards.back: scale back — reduce in scope: We scaled back the pilot to two sites. roll out — deploy progressively: The new procedure will be rolled out in Q3. factor in — include in a calculation: Have you factored in the downtime? bring forward — move to an earlier date: The audit has been brought forward to April. (Its opposite is push back: The deadline was pushed back a week.) see through — carry to completion: She saw the project through despite the cuts.

cards.front: Writing a recommendation that gets acted on
cards.back: Three moves, in this order: 1. The recommendation itself, first and unhedged. We recommend replacing the seals on all four units before the summer peak. 2. The reasoning, quantified. Two of the four have exceeded 8,000 hours, and a failure in service costs roughly ten times a planned replacement. 3. The alternative and why it loses. Deferring to the autumn shutdown would save the labour cost but leaves the units running through the highest-load period. ⚠️ Burying the recommendation under the analysis is the most common reason a good report changes nothing.

cards.front: VOCABULARY — quantifying findings precisely
cards.back: The failure rate rose sharply / edged up / plateaued / tailed off. Roughly a third of the units were affected. — approximate Just under 40 % / Well over half — a direction with the number The difference was negligible / marginal / substantial. Consumption fell by 12 % to 44 litres. — by = the change, to = the result ⚠️ Fell to 12 % and fell by 12 % mean completely different things.

cards.front: A client writes an angry email about a defect. Which opening is most professional?
choices: Thank you for flagging this — I understand the disruption this has caused, and I've already asked the workshop for the inspection records.
We are not responsible for this defect as our terms clearly state…
Sorry!! This should never have happened, it's completely our fault.
Please note that your email has been received and will be processed.
cards.back: It does three things at once: acknowledges without admitting liability, names the impact (which is what the client actually wants heard), and states a concrete action already taken. The second is defensive, the third concedes liability before the facts are known, and the fourth is a wall of process language that reads as indifference.

cards.front: Third person singular takes an -s: «She {{works}} here», but the negative drops it: «She doesn't {{work}} here».
cards.back: The -s moves to the auxiliary, so it never appears twice.

cards.front: To {{look}} after someone is to take care of them; to {{look}} into something is to investigate it.
cards.back: Same verb, different particle, completely different meaning.

cards.front: How do you say «archivo adjunto» in English?
cards.back: Attachment
